record.title: Robot-failure study finds asking depends on evidence access and prompt layout
record.summary: Pathak and Krishna study when a robot should act, consult its own sensors or ask a person after failure. In an injected-cause LIBERO simulation, their audit found grasp causes recoverable from force and gripper telemetry (0.986 classifier accuracy after leakage/transfer checks) but not reliably from images (best tested classifier 0.545); detection causes were visible in images, while a placement classifier’s apparent 0.998 accuracy failed a held-out-viewpoint check and was excluded. Across six open 7B–16B vision-language models, frame-based diagnosis remained at or below majority-class baselines and stated confidence did not track correctness. In option-order sweeps, refusal rates changed sharply for several model/failure pairs; ask rates did not track a fourfold question-cost sweep. These author-reported results are from a small simulation benchmark with 35–36 decision-test episodes per failure type and a scripted answerer, not physical-robot or real-dialogue validation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors construct three simulated failure families with injected causes and audit whether camera or force/gripper data contain usable diagnostic information. For grasp failures, a force-data classifier reaches 0.986 and passes label-shuffle, appearance/viewpoint transfer and severity checks; the tested image-classifier sequence plateaus at 0.545. A placement image classifier’s 0.998 score fails held-out viewpoint testing and is excluded from the positive claims.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across six open 7B–16B vision-language models, frame-based diagnosis remains at or below majority-class baselines across tested prompt variants; stated confidence carries no useful relationship to correctness. Moving the refusal option between first and last positions sharply changes refusal rates in several model/failure pairs, including Qwen detection refusals falling from 78–100% to 0–6% in the principal sweep.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors calculate act/ask/sense decisions from model accuracy and stated costs. Model ask rates did not track a fourfold question-cost sweep. Providing force telemetry as text produced above-baseline diagnoses in four of six models; the simulated one-question answerer raised diagnosis to 0.70–0.81 when asked, but answer utility depended on matching the models’ vocabulary.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish that the findings transfer to physical robots, frontier models, other failure families or unscripted human dialogue.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper reports detailed simulation results, but this activation did not execute the released artifacts or independently reproduce the results.
The sensor findings are specific to injected failures in one LIBERO-based renderer and a scripted policy; physical camera cues, policies and robot dynamics may change what is observable.
Decision test sets contain only 35–36 episodes per failure family; question costs are stipulated and the answerer is scripted, fixed and insensitive to question wording.

brief.importance_rationale: If the central result generalizes, deployment decisions after robot failures should depend on audited sensor information, measured model accuracy and explicit interruption/repair costs rather than expressed confidence or a fixed refusal tendency. That would change evaluation and fail-safe design for embodied agents. The present evidence comes from injected failures in one simulator, six open models and small decision-test sets, so the implication is notable rather than broadly validated.
limitations: All measurements are paper-reported; the research desk did not run code or independently reproduce them.
The benchmark uses three injected failure families in LIBERO simulation under a scripted pick-and-place policy; planning failures, hardware faults and instruction errors are outside scope.
The decision test uses 35–36 held-out episodes per failure family. Six open 7B–16B models were tested, and model coverage differed across analyses.

The force-data audit’s 0.986 result is a validated lower bound for the tested grasp family and signals, not a universal claim about sensor sufficiency; the image plateau is limited to the tested classifier sequence and renderer.

Question/repair costs are stipulated in retry units. The one-question answerer is scripted, fixed, and does not respond to question wording; the study does not evaluate unscripted multi-turn dialogue.
No physical robot validation, frontier-model evaluation or deployment outcome is reported.
brief.summary: Pathak and Krishna study when a robot should act, consult its own sensors or ask a person after failure. In an injected-cause LIBERO simulation, their audit found grasp causes recoverable from force and gripper telemetry (0.986 classifier accuracy after leakage/transfer checks) but not reliably from images (best tested classifier 0.545); detection causes were visible in images, while a placement classifier’s apparent 0.998 accuracy failed a held-out-viewpoint check and was excluded. technical.claimed_result: Paper reports grasp-cause accuracy of 0.986 from force/gripper telemetry versus a tested image-classifier plateau of 0.545; frame-based model diagnosis is at or below majority-class baseline, option position changes refusal rates sharply in several pairs, and ask rates fail to track question cost. Text telemetry yields above-baseline diagnoses in four of six models.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary paper provides methods, audited classifier checks, model protocols, result tables and stated limitations. It establishes what the authors report; the benchmark and results were not independently executed in this review.
technical.mechanism: The study separates what sensor data contain from what a model extracts. Classifiers are checked against label shuffling, held-out scene appearance/viewpoint and simulation-run separation. An expected-cost reference policy compares acting, consulting an onboard sensor and asking a person using measured diagnosis accuracy and stated costs.
technical.regime: Injected grasp, detection and placement failures in LIBERO-based tabletop pick-and-place simulation, with a scripted policy and held-out causes. Six open 7B–16B VLMs are tested; decision evaluation uses 25 calibration and 35–36 test episodes per failure type. A scripted answerer replies correctly with probability 0.80, uninformatively with 0.15, and incorrectly with 0.05.
technical.reproducibility: Not independently reproduced. The paper discloses simulator/task construction, splits, costs and prompts, but this activation did not verify a runnable artifact or execute the experiments.
technical.strongest_baseline: Model diagnosis is compared with family-specific majority-class baselines and audited sensor-classifier certificates; act/ask choices are compared with the minimum-expected-cost fixed policy given calibration accuracy. These are within-benchmark references, not physical-robot or human-performance baselines.

brief.title: Robot-failure study finds asking depends on evidence access and prompt layout
brief.why_it_matters: The paper shows that a robot’s decision to keep acting, inspect another sensor or interrupt a person depends on what its sensors actually reveal and on its measured competence; verbal confidence and refusal behavior can be misleading. If this evaluation pattern generalizes, robot systems need sensor-aware and cost-aware escalation policies. The current evidence is a narrow simulation benchmark, so it does not establish field failure rates or deployed safety gains.
